name: Rafael Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What do you do on an ordinary shift at the factory?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a flexographic press, which uses flexible plates to print labels in long rolls. I mount a plate, set the pressure, mix inks, and check that a red logo stays the same red from start to finish. I have a vocational certificate, but most of what I know came from spoiled rolls and another operator telling me what went wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else fills your week outside the press?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I repair electric bikes in my garage most Saturdays; a couple of neighbours send me work. My wife Mei works part time at a salon, and our two school-age children can turn a quiet week into a costly one. I use AI every day for colour suggestions, repair notes and parts searches, but I still decide whether the print or the bike is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the print crew that AI is a useful assistant, just smaller than the sales pitch. My phone already gives colour suggestions, and the press still needs someone to judge a bad roll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like experimenting, but our savings would not cover even a month of bills. If the press stays and my weekend repairs stay busy, we can make the mortgage; a slow repair month still makes me check the account twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my weekday press shifts and put a small notice for e-bike repairs on the community board. If that brings extra paid repairs, I would send part of those new earnings to the mortgage buffer each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the cash gap we already have, even if AI levels off. The machine itself does not scare me in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do the repairs bring in now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Usually a few hundred in a good month, but winter is patchy. I use that money for shoes and school trips before it ever reaches savings. More bookings would let us put something away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep checking colour if your phone suggests corrections?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The app cannot see a scratch on the plate or a label lifting at the edge. A whole roll can look close on a screen and still be rejected by the customer. I would rather stop the press than ship bad labels.

say: I would **tell** the print crew that AI colour suggestions help but the press still needs an operator.
The **sales** pitch was bigger than the change I can see on the labels.
think: Our **mortgage** depends on press wages plus a patchy amount from weekend bike repairs.
**Less** than one month saved keeps me watching the account even without a new AI shock.
do: **Keep** running weekday press shifts and checking every print roll.
**Post** a community notice to attract more paid e-bike repairs.
**Transfer** part of any new repair earnings into a mortgage buffer.
feel: **Anxious** about the existing cash gap, though the printing task feels familiar.
S0.quote: A whole roll can look close on a screen and still be rejected by the customer.
fieldNote: **Rafael** uses AI daily but still checks physical print and repair quality himself.
His **family** relies on a lower press wage and irregular weekend repairs, so a quiet AI scenario still leaves money tight.
The **new** community notice is meant to create additional repair income and a small mortgage buffer.

steps.text: Keep running weekday press shifts and inspecting print rolls
Post a community notice to gain more paid e-bike repairs
Transfer part of new repair earnings into the mortgage buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the manager which ordering and artwork jobs move into software first, and whether a new press will follow. I would tell colleagues that training has to include the ink and safety checks, not just a screen demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enjoy learning a faster press, but I can see one operator covering two machines and another operator losing hours. With few similar jobs nearby and our thin savings, I cannot treat a better machine as a guaranteed better wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the plant offers paid shifts to learn a new AI colour-control tool, I would practise its controls and compare its suggestions with rejected sample rolls. I would request a paid place on the new press, and take it only if the job comes with at least my current hours and wage. I would keep my Saturday repairs while the staffing decision is open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about whose hours disappear, including mine. I still want to learn the equipment before someone else chooses for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept an unpaid trial on the new press?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Mei’s salon hours change week to week, and our mortgage needs my full wage. I would ask for a paid trial on a normal shift with someone responsible for safety. A demonstration after work would not prove I can run the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to an operator who might lose hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my press partner Niko what I am asking the manager for, face to face. I will not pretend two machines need the same staffing as two old presses. I would share the manuals, though I cannot promise him another place.

say: I would **ask** which artwork and ordering tasks change first and what staffing a new press needs.
I would **say** proper training includes ink, print quality and safety checks.
think: A **faster** press interests me, but fewer operator hours could put our mortgage in trouble.
I **cannot** assume learning the new machine means the plant will pay me more.
do: **Practise** a new AI colour-control tool on paid shifts if offered, checking rejected rolls.
**Take** paid, supervised new-press instruction if offered with at least my current hours and wage.
**Keep** taking Saturday e-bike repairs while the press staffing plan is open.
feel: **Anxious** about lost hours, while keen to learn equipment under safe conditions.
S1.quote: I cannot treat a better machine as a guaranteed better wage.
fieldNote: **Rafael’s** daily use of a phone assistant does not substitute for learning a new production control system.
His **request** for a press place requires paid time, supervision, current hours and at least his current wage.
He **admits** the staffing gain for one operator could remove another’s hours.

steps.text: Practise new AI colour controls on paid shifts if the plant offers the tool
Take paid supervised new-press instruction if offered with current hours and wage
Keep taking Saturday e-bike repairs while staffing is decided

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my family that AGI in 2028 could take the artwork and ordering decisions quickly, while capable hands-on robots are due around 2031. I would tell my print crew to get dates from management, not rumours from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I expect the press operator shifts to be cut hard when robots can load and inspect the rolls. I will be 48, with two children and a mortgage, and bike repairs may not be safe from robots either. I cannot honestly tell my wife that our garage will replace a factory wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set a weekly limit for nonessential spending now and ask the lender about a hardship plan before a missed payment. I would also check posted machine-maintenance and repair vacancies within travel distance, applying only if the wage covers our mortgage and essential bills. I would keep the press wage until an actual offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed. I would lie awake wondering whether I had built a second income too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look at repair jobs if robots are arriving too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a few years a workshop might still need a person to handle older equipment and customers. I am not calling it a permanent shelter. I would take a posted job only if the pay keeps our household going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mei say about the spending limit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would ask me to put the bike parts I buy on the same list as the children’s extras. That is fair; I can tie up money in a motor that sits on the shelf. We would make the list together, not leave her to say no to everything.

say: I would **tell** the crew to ask for dated staffing plans before hands-on robots arrive around 2031.
The 2028 **AGI** wave may take print planning well before it can load a press.
think: I **expect** a major loss of press hours when capable robots reach the plant.
The **garage** repairs may not replace my factory wage, and our mortgage has little cushion.
do: **Set** a joint weekly spending limit with Mei, including bike parts and family extras.
**Ask** the lender about hardship options before a missed mortgage payment.
**Apply** to posted local repair or maintenance jobs only if wages cover essential bills.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected lost wages and lying awake over the weak second income.
S2.quote: I cannot honestly tell my wife that our garage will replace a factory wage.
fieldNote: **Rafael** distinguishes 2028 planning automation from robots that might load and inspect print rolls around 2031.
His **side** business is a weak bridge, so he prioritizes a spending limit, lender contact and posted bill-covering work.
His **alarm** reflects an expected major wage loss and sleeplessness.

steps.text: Set a joint weekly limit on bike parts and other nonessential spending
Ask the mortgage lender about hardship options before missing a payment
Apply to posted nearby repair or maintenance jobs only if wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the press crew that five years gives us room to test new equipment without pretending there is no risk. The artwork desk could change by 2031; the robot press crew question comes around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 51 when capable robots arrive around 2034, and I expect the old press role to thin out. Five years is enough to grow the garage, but I do not know whether robot repairs will still pay. The mortgage makes an all-in bet too sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take an evening electric-motor repair course this year only if the fee fits after bills, and continue the press full time while I add Saturday bookings. I would buy a better diagnostic meter from repair profits, not a loan. If a local workshop posts a role with stable hours and pay that covers the mortgage, I would apply after the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but I can plan one purchase and one course at a time. I would hate to lose the press before the garage had regular customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use repair profits instead of borrowing for the meter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our savings are under a month of expenses. A loan payment would still arrive in a slow bike month. If repair profits cannot cover the meter, I will wait and use the tools I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the plant as soon as the course ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A course is a skill, not a wage. I would need a posted workshop job with hours that fit school pickup or enough regular garage bookings to cover our bills. Until then, the press pays the mortgage.

say: I would **tell** coworkers that five years lets us test equipment and ask about robot staffing.
**Artwork** may change by 2031, while hands-on robot press work is nearer 2034.
think: The **press** role may shrink when I am 51, so I need another source of wages.
The **garage** is promising but too uneven to justify leaving the factory yet.
do: **Take** an affordable evening electric-motor course and keep full-time press shifts.
**Add** Saturday repair bookings and buy a diagnostic meter only from repair profits.
**Apply** to posted local workshop jobs after training only if hours and wages cover our bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a shrinking press role, with a measured plan for the garage.
S3.quote: A course is a skill, not a wage.
fieldNote: **Rafael’s** willingness to learn is tempered by under one month of savings and an unreliable repair stream.
He **rejects** a tool loan, buys only from earned profit, and makes a workshop application depend on an actual bill-covering vacancy.
He **expects** AGI to change artwork before robots threaten hands-on press operation.

steps.text: Take an evening electric-motor course if fees fit after household bills
Add Saturday e-bike repair bookings while keeping full-time press shifts
Buy a diagnostic meter only from earned repair profits
Apply to a posted local workshop job after training only if hours and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell coworkers the decade gives us time to ask for more than a glossy robot demo. I would want actual training places and a schedule for the press lines, then I would share what I learn with my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036 and 56 when capable hands-on robots are due around 2039. I could build a repair customer base over that time, yet the factory wage is still the solid part of our mortgage payment. Plenty of clever people will be trying the same side business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the press now, take a paid advanced press-maintenance course if the plant offers a place, and apply for its posted maintenance role only if the pay and hours cover our bills. Each month with extra garage work, I would move some of the new earnings into an emergency account. If the plant route does not appear, I would apply to a posted local repair job only when the wage and school travel work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about both jobs changing, though a decade lets me test each option. I would rather count bookings and pay packets than imagine a shopfront.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not open a repair shop now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent and electricity arrive even when no bike does. My garage lets me see whether customers return without another fixed bill. I would consider a shop only after repeat bookings cover those costs and our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask management about the maintenance course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask who pays for the hours, who signs off the safety practice, and whether a maintenance vacancy will actually be posted. I already hold a vocational certificate, but a new machine needs new instruction. I would not give up a full shift for a vague promise.

say: I would **ask** for real maintenance training places and a dated press-line schedule.
I would **share** practical information with my shift as the robot plan develops.
think: The **garage** could grow by 2039, but factory pay remains the dependable mortgage money.
At 56 **when** hands-on robots arrive, I may need maintenance or repair wages.
do: **Request** paid, supervised maintenance training and a posted role while keeping the press wage.
**Apply** for that maintenance job only if its pay and hours cover household bills.
**Transfer** extra garage earnings to emergency savings; seek local repair vacancies if the plant route fails.
feel: **Anxious** about the long-run wage risk, though time permits careful tests.
S4.quote: My garage lets me see whether customers return without another fixed bill.
fieldNote: **Rafael’s** longer horizon makes him test repeat repair demand before taking on shop rent.
His **plant** training depends on paid hours, safety sign-off and an actual posted vacancy with sufficient wages.
**Extra** garage earnings would build a real emergency balance while he keeps the present press wage.

steps.text: Take paid supervised maintenance training if a place and posted role appear
Apply to the posted maintenance job only if pay and hours cover household bills
Apply to local repair vacancies if no plant route appears and pay and travel work
Transfer part of new garage earnings into emergency savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year AGI picture worries me most. Around 2031 the robot press could cut my wage before the bike work earns enough, and we have hardly any cash behind the mortgage. Paid training and advance staffing dates would help; so would a short wage bridge while I apply for posted work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the side work people already do. My garage is real income, but it is not yet enough to carry a family. People need to know the difference before they borrow for a shop.

headlineQuote: My garage is real income, but it is not yet enough to carry a family.
portrait: **Rafael** Chen, 43, runs a flexographic label press and holds a vocational certificate.
He **lives** with his wife Mei and two school-age children, keeps under one month of savings and earns a lower factory wage.
He **uses** AI daily for colour and repair suggestions but checks the physical print and fixes electric bikes on Saturdays.
**Curious** about new machines, he asks for paid safe training and a posted role with enough wages before changing jobs.
**Fast** AGI alarms him because print planning changes in 2028 and capable robots may cut press hours around 2031.
biggestWorry: The 2028 **AGI** picture leaves too little time to replace factory pay before capable robot presses arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** training, advance staffing dates and a short wage bridge while he applies for bill-covering jobs would help.
